lines.cap: **Narrator:** This is Kavya. She is twelve. It is Saturday, and she has science homework.
**Kavya:** 'Find twenty things in your kitchen. Element, compound or mixture?' On a Saturday.
**Kavya:** Most of our kitchen is a mixture. Of my brother's dirty bowls.
**Narrator:** But this documentary is not about Kavya. It is about something much, much smaller.
**Narrator:** Above her noodles drift billions of atoms. Some are looking for a partner.
**Narrator:** And this is where they come to find one.
**Arthur:** Hi. Arthur. **Argon**. I run the agency.
**Arthur:** I find atoms their perfect match. They bond. Happily ever after.
**Arthur:** Me? No. I'm a **noble gas**. I hardly react with anything. I don't bond.
**Arthur:** My name literally means 'lazy', in Greek.
**Arthur:** I've been single for about four billion years. It's going great.
**Narrator:** Happily Ever Atom. Episode six: Just Flatmates.
**Narrator:** Nine a.m. The agency opens. Every client is single: an **element**.
**Arthur:** An **element** is made of only **one type of atom**. Gold? Only gold atoms.
**Arthur:** There are about **118** of them, all in our catalogue: the **periodic table**.
**Arthur:** An element **can't be broken down** into anything simpler by a chemical reaction.
**Nate:** HI! I'm Nate! **Sodium**! A soft, shiny metal, and I am SO ready to bond!
**Arthur:** Nate is sodium. Very reactive. Banned from every pool in Singapore.
**Nate:** Name: Nate! **Chemical symbol**: N, A!
**Arthur:** Small a.
**Arthur:** The **first letter is always a capital**. A **second letter is always lower case**.
**Arthur:** **Big then small**. Sodium is **Na**. Magnesium is **Mg**. Carbon is just **C**.
**Arthur:** It matters. The metal **cobalt** is **Co**. But **CO** is **carbon monoxide**: carbon and oxygen, bonded.
**Arthur:** Two capitals isn't a client. It's a couple.
**Chloe:** Hello. I'm Chloe. **Chlorine**. A poisonous green gas.
**Chloe:** I'm toxic. It's not a personality. It's a fact.
**Arthur:** A metal that explodes in water. A poisonous gas. On paper, a disaster. In chemistry? Perfect.
**Narrator:** When atoms of **two or more different elements** are **chemically bonded** together, they make a **compound**.
**Nate:** Here we go! Bonding in three, two, one!
**Sal:** Hey. I'm Sal. **Sodium chloride**. Table salt.
**Sal:** I go on food. I love it there.
**Kavya:** Wait. Where did the explosive one and the poisonous one go?
**Arthur:** Still in there. But a **compound** has **different properties** from the elements that make it.
**Arthur:** One sodium for every chlorine. Always. A **fixed ratio**. The **formula** is **NaCl**.
**Narrator:** Same with water. Hydrogen's an explosive gas. Oxygen helps things burn. Bonded, as **water**, they put fires out.
**Arthur:** Its formula: **H₂O**. The little two counts the atom before it: two hydrogens. No number means one oxygen.
**Arthur:** **Carbon dioxide** is **CO₂**. Forget the little two, and you've written carbon monoxide.
**Arthur:** Splitting a compound back up takes a **chemical reaction**. Not easy.
**Sal:** Relax. We're not splitting up.
**Narrator:** Meanwhile, at Arthur's flat. It's in the air. Literally.
**Nigel & Nigel:** Hello. I'm Nigel.
**Nigel & Nigel:** And I'm also Nigel.
**Arthur:** My flatmates. Two **nitrogen** atoms, joined: a **molecule**.
**Narrator:** A **molecule** is **two or more atoms joined** by chemical bonds.
**Kavya:** So they're bonded. That makes them a compound, right?
**Arthur:** No.
**Arthur:** Both nitrogen. Same type of atom, so still an **element**, like **O₂**. A compound needs **different** elements.
**Nigel & Nigel:** We get that a lot.
**Narrator:** In **particle pictures**, each circle is an atom, and its **colour** shows its type.
**Arthur:** Ask two things. Same atoms, or different? Joined, or just mixed?
**Arthur:** All the same: **element**. Different, and bonded: **compound**. Different, but not bonded to each other: **mixture**. **Same, Bonded, Free**.
**Arthur:** And air? A **mixture**. **78%** nitrogen, **21%** oxygen, about **1%** argon: me. Nobody's bonded to their flatmates. We just share.
**Narrator:** **Sea water** is a mixture. So are **alloys**: **brass** is copper and zinc, **steel** is iron and carbon.
**Kavya:** Brass looks like one metal, though.
**Arthur:** It's a mixture in a very convincing costume.

**Arthur:** So. **Compound**: bonded, **fixed ratio**, needs a **chemical reaction** to split. **Mixture**: not bonded, each keeps its **own properties**, **any ratio**, separated by **physical methods**.
**Kavya:** My juice carton says 'one hundred percent pure'. See? Pure.
**Arthur:** In chemistry, **pure** means **one element or one compound**, and nothing else. Your juice? A delicious mixture.
**Narrator:** Test purity with a **melting point**. A pure substance melts at **one sharp temperature**: pure ice, at exactly **0 °C**.
**Sal:** Add me, and I'm an **impurity**. The **melting point goes down**, the **boiling point goes up**, and both spread over a **range**.
**Sal:** That's why cold countries spread me on icy roads.
**Kavya:** We don't have icy roads. It's thirty-four degrees.
**Kavya:** He's gone! He disappeared!
**Arthur:** He hasn't disappeared. He's **dissolved**.
**Arthur:** Sal's the **solute**: what dissolves. Water's the **solvent**: the liquid it's in. Together: a **solution**.
**Arthur:** **10 g** of salt plus **100 g** of water: **110 g** of solution. Nothing destroyed.
**Sandy:** Hi. Sandy. Sand. I'm **insoluble**. Everyone else goes for a swim. I just sit at the bottom.
**Narrator:** Keep adding salt, and eventually no more dissolves. The solution is **saturated**.
**Arthur:** The most that can dissolve in a fixed amount of solvent is its **solubility**. It usually **rises with temperature**.
**Kavya:** That's why there's always sugar at the bottom of my iced teh-O!
**Arthur:** Partly. Also, stir it.
**Arthur:** **Concentration**: how much solute is in a given volume. **Few** particles: **dilute**. **Many**: **concentrated**.
**Kavya:** So teh-O siew dai, less sugar, is more **dilute**.
**Narrator:** Eviction night. Kavya's beaker of muddy, salty water must be separated.
**Arthur:** **Filtration** separates an **insoluble solid** from a **liquid**. Pour it through **filter paper** in a funnel.
**Sandy:** Oh. Oh no. I'm stuck. I'm stuck in the paper.
**Arthur:** Sand's too big for the paper's holes. What stays on the paper: the **residue**. What passes through: the **filtrate**.
**Sandy:** Residue. They even gave me a sad name.
**Sal:** Bye, Sandy! I'm going straight through!
**Arthur:** Dissolved particles slip right through. You **can't filter salt out of salt water**.
**Narrator:** To get a dissolved solid back, heat it. The water **evaporates**. The salt is left behind.
**Arthur:** For neater crystals, **crystallisation**: heat until it's **saturated**, then **cool slowly**. **Filter** off the crystals, and **dry** them.
**Sal:** Ta-da! Crystals! I'm a cube again!
**Narrator:** To get the water back, use **simple distillation**. The water **boils** into vapour. The salt stays behind.
**Arthur:** In the **condenser**, the vapour **cools** and **condenses** back into pure water.
**Arthur:** So: **evaporation keeps the solid**. **Distillation keeps the liquid**.
**Narrator:** **Fractional distillation** separates liquids with **different boiling points**, like crude oil. The **lowest boiling point** comes off first, at the top.
**Arthur:** They did that to my flat once. Cooled the air to a liquid, then boiled us off one at a time.
**Nigel & Nigel:** We came off first. Lowest boiling point. Very proud.
**Narrator:** Back home, a crime. Someone drank Kavya's bubble tea and left a note.
**Kavya:** 'Sorry.' In black ink. Three suspects. One of them is my brother.
**Inky:** Hey hey! I'm Inky! Black ink! Just one colour. Very mysterious.
**Narrator:** **Chromatography** separates **coloured substances**, like the dyes in an ink.
**Arthur:** Spot the ink on a **pencil line** near the bottom. Stand the paper in a **solvent**, the spot just **above** it.
**Narrator:** The solvent soaks up. Each dye travels a **different distance**, depending on how **soluble** it is and how much it **sticks to the paper**.
**Inky:** Wait. Why am I splitting up? I'm blue! And pink! And yellow?!
**Arthur:** Inky thought she was one colour. Turns out, she's a mixture. Big day for her.
**Arthur:** Now run each suspect's pen alongside. If spots end up **level**, they're very likely the **same substance**.
**Kavya:** My brother's pen. Every spot, level. I KNEW it.
**Narrator:** **Oil and water** don't mix: they're **immiscible**. They form **layers**, the less dense oil on top.
**Arthur:** In a **separating funnel**, open the **tap**: the **lower layer** drains first. Close it at the boundary.
**Narrator:** If one solid is **magnetic**, like **iron filings** in sand, a **magnet** lifts it out.
**Sandy:** Great. Now even the iron is leaving me.
**Arthur:** Only magnetic metals: **iron**, **steel**, **nickel** and **cobalt**. Small o.
**Arthur:** Solids, liquids, or dissolved? Do they mix? Anything magnetic? **Match the method to the mixture**.
**Arthur:** Matching. It's what I do.

chapters.title: The cast saves you some marks

lines.cap: **Narrator:** Before the credits, the cast would like to save you marks.
**Nate:** One! **Big then small**! Sodium is **Na**, not NA. Two capitals means two elements!
**Chloe:** Two. A compound has **different properties** from its elements. I was poison gas. Now I'm on chips.
**Nigel & Nigel:** Three. Identical atoms joined together are still an **element**. We're both Nigel.
**Sal:** Four. Dissolved isn't destroyed. I'm still there, and my **mass is conserved**.
**Sandy:** Five. You **can't filter** salt out of salt water. Only I get stuck.
**Arthur:** Six. **Evaporation** keeps the solid. **Distillation** keeps the liquid.
**Inky:** Seven! Impurities **lower** the melting point, and spread it over a **range**!
**Narrator:** Happily Ever Atom will return.
**Nigel & Nigel:** Arthur. We've found you a match.
**Arthur:** Nigel. I'm a noble gas. I don't bond.
**Nigel & Nigel:** It's another argon atom.
**Arthur:** ...Fine. We'll be flatmates.
